summary: Registers a media type for the Material Exchange Format, defined by SMPTE 377M. MXF is a wrapper format for exchanging audiovisual material, carrying both the audio and video data and rich descriptive metadata. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: A movie file needs a box that holds the pictures, the sound and a label describing them. MXF is that box, and this memo gives the box an official internet name.

questions: what video formats does mxf support
subtitle: An Internet media type for exchanging audiovisual files with metadata.

tldr.problem: Video and audio files need a standard way to be identified over the Internet, and they need to carry not just the audiovisual material but also rich descriptive metadata about that content.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers the media type application/mxf for the Material Exchange Format (MXF) defined by SMPTE 377M, a container format that wraps both audiovisual essence and structural and descriptive metadata together.
tldr.outcome: The registration allows MXF files to be correctly identified and handled when served over HTTP, included in multi-part documents, or indexed by systems, with an optional parameter to hint at file structure using SMPTE Universal Labels.

today: RFC 4539 is an Informational memo that registers the media type for MXF, the Material Exchange Format used in broadcast and digital cinema. The registration is in current use, and systems continue to exchange audiovisual material using this container format with its rich metadata capabilities.

sections.title: What MXF Is and Why It Matters
sections.content:
The Material Exchange Format (MXF), defined by SMPTE 377M, is a standard wrapper format for packaging audiovisual material during interchange between systems. It carries both the raw audiovisual data (called essence) and rich metadata that describes the material.

MXF is used widely in broadcast and digital cinema systems, in non-linear editing, video servers, cameras, digital asset management, and video distribution. The format is important because it allows video systems from different vendors to exchange material reliably while preserving both the content and all the information about that content.

This RFC registers an official Internet media type for MXF so that systems can correctly identify and handle MXF files when they are served over HTTP, included in email attachments or multi-part documents, or indexed by operating systems and asset management systems.
sections.plainLanguage: MXF is like a special box for moving movie files between companies. The box holds the pictures and sound, but also carries a label with all the details. This memo gives that box an official name so the Internet knows what it is.

sections.title: Essence and Metadata
sections.content:
MXF wraps two kinds of data. The essence is the raw video, audio, and data streams—the actual media. The metadata describes the essence in two layers.

Structural metadata describes how the MXF file is organized and is required for proper decoding. Examples include descriptions of essence types, synchronization information for playout of audio and video, and content length. Descriptive metadata gives information about the program content itself, such as title, actors, and scene descriptions, but is not essential for decoding.

The format is flexible: essence itself may carry additional data, such as vertical blanking interval data used for Closed Captioning and other purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: The box holds two kinds of information. First is the actual picture and sound. Second is a description: what the movie is called, who is in it, and how long it is. Both go in the same box.

sections.title: The Media Type Registration
sections.content:
The registered media type is application/mxf. MXF files use the file extension .mxf.

An optional parameter called ULs (Universal Labels) provides hints about the structure of the MXF file to a decoder. This single Uniform Resource Name (URN), or comma-separated list of URNs, can indicate the Operational Pattern of the file, the essence types it contains, descriptive metadata schemes, and other elements identified by SMPTE Universal Labels. These labels are Object Identifiers (OIDs). For example, an MXF file using OP1a Operational Pattern with IEC DV video would be labeled with two Universal Labels indicating both the pattern and the video type.

The media type is for binary content and carries no required parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet name for an MXF file is application/mxf, and files end in .mxf. You can optionally add a label describing what kind of video is inside, so the player knows what to expect.

sections.title: Supporting Diverse Essence Types
sections.content:
SMPTE defines mappings for many essence types to the MXF generic container. Supported types include MPEG (MPEG-1 and MPEG-2 video, MPEG audio), DV-DIF (Digital Video Digital Interface Format), uncompressed pictures, SDTI-CP (Serial Digital Transport Interface Content Package), D-10 (a specialized MPEG-2 4:2:2 video stream), D-11 (high-definition video compression), AES3 audio, Broadcast Wave audio, and A-Law audio.

The flexibility of the MXF generic container allows for future mappings of additional essence types to be defined by SMPTE. This makes MXF adaptable as video technologies and compression standards evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: MXF can hold many different kinds of video and audio—from old-fashioned uncompressed video to modern compressed formats. When new video formats are invented, MXF can be updated to hold them too.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
MXF objects are not signed but may be partially encrypted internally. External security mechanisms such as TLS should be used to ensure content confidentiality when transmitting MXF files.

Through metadata extensions, MXF may allow executable code to be transferred in the file. It is recommended that unauthenticated executables decoded from an MXF file should not be executed without verification.

Some compressed essence types may carry a risk that certain pathological bitstreams could cause denial-of-service attacks against the essence decoders themselves.

Interoperability depends on whether both encoder and decoder support the same Operational Pattern (OP) and essence types. An Application Specification (AS) can ensure effective interoperability between MXF encoders and decoders.
sections.plainLanguage: When moving sensitive movies, you should encrypt them with additional protection. Don't run any programs that come hidden in the file without checking they are safe first. Different video players might not understand all types of MXF files.
